name: Ceramide EOP

lead: Ceramide EOP is one of the skin's own ceramides, lipids that help hold water in the outer skin layer. The payoff is skin that stays hydrated and calm, so it looks smoother and less dry.

Ceramides sit in the lipid matrix between skin cells alongside cholesterol and fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss. Most of what is known comes from ceramides as a group; published material on this particular subtype is thin.

paras: It appears in barrier-repair moisturisers and creams, typically alongside cholesterol and fatty acids and used daily on dry or sensitive skin. Hydration effects show up quickly, with barrier improvement over weeks.
It is a cosmetic ingredient and ceramide products are generally well tolerated. No subtype-specific safety findings were located.

angle.text: Ceramide EOP is a barrier lipid found in repair moisturisers. It helps skin hold water, so dry, rough skin looks smoother and calmer. Research is mostly on ceramides as a group rather than this subtype.

lead: Ceramide EOP is a skin-identical ceramide listed on the ingredient labels of barrier-repair moisturisers. People use ceramide creams to keep skin hydrated, smooth and comfortable, since a well-supported skin barrier looks less dry, flaky and irritated.[1]

Ceramides are waxy lipids made of sphingosine joined to a fatty acid by an amide bond. In the outer skin layer, the stratum corneum, dead cells sit in a lipid matrix often described as bricks and mortar, and ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids form the mortar that limits evaporative water loss and helps block microorganisms.[1] As a rule of thumb the mix is roughly half ceramides by weight, about a quarter cholesterol and about 15 percent free fatty acids.[1]

Skin ceramide levels are reported to fall with dry or polluted air, harsh sulfate cleansers, heat, UV exposure and ageing, which is the logic behind adding them back topically.[1] Published coverage of ceramide EOP as a named subtype is sparse; the broader literature concerns ceramides as a class.

paras: Ceramides are lipids built from sphingosine and a fatty acid. Epidermal ceramides are grouped into classes by structure, and the Wikipedia article names AS and NS ceramides, ADS and NDS dihydroceramides, AH, EOH and NH 6-hydroxyceramides, AP and NP phytoceramides, and EOH and EOS acylceramides; it does not discuss EOP by name.[1]
Ceramide profiles vary by body site, with thin, flexible facial skin differing from thick, rigid heel skin.[1]

Ceramides appear in cosmetics including soaps, shampoos, skin creams and sunscreens, and some topical skin medications contain ceramides to complement eczema treatment.[1] Ceramide-containing moisturisers are marketed for dry or compromised skin, and ceramide EOP is one of several ceramide types listed in such formulas.

In psoriasis, AS and NS ceramides increase while EOS, AP and NP ceramides decrease, which may weaken the water barrier.[1] One study of atopic dermatitis and psoriasis found that sphingoid base and fatty-acid chain length influenced whether a ceramide was up- or down-regulated more than its class did, and a 2022 JCI Insight study reported site- and disease-specific changes in epidermal lipids.[1]

No studies found on ceramide EOP specifically. The Wikipedia article on ceramides cites research on the composition of ceramides in psoriatic scale (1993), reviews of ceramides and skin function (2003), epidermal lipids and barrier homeostasis (2007) and the microstructure of the stratum corneum lipid barrier (2010), but gives no efficacy data for moisturisers.[1]
